beats.narration_text: Someone asked if Claude approves a vendor's DPA when it reviews one. Wrong verb — approving would be a judgment. Claude runs a fixed clause list instead, one check at a time. So: is it checking a list?

beats.narration_text: Here's what a Skill actually is: a folder Claude reads before it acts. This one's called dpa-review, and its one file — SKILL.md — holds the whole instruction set in plain language. No hidden logic, no side channel. Claude reads the file, then acts. They optimized for one thing: you should be able to read the program by opening the file. The file is the program.

The instructions live in a Steps section. Claude reads each step in order and executes it — read the file, run each step, return the result. Linear on purpose: no branching unless a step says otherwise. That choice buys you predictability at the expense of cleverness. You always know what it'll do next, because the next line tells you.

production_viz.label: READ, EXECUTE, RETURN
production_viz.caption: linear — no branching unless a step says so

beats.narration_text: One check inside it is very specific — does the agreement name every sub-processor, and does it say what happens to the data when the contract ends: deleted, or returned. Those two clauses go missing more often than any other. Here's what the skill doesn't do: judge whether the described security measures are actually strong enough for the data at stake. That's a judgment call, and it needs a person who knows both the systems and the risk. They optimized for coverage over verdict — the skill tells you what's missing; whether what's there is any good is still on you.

production_viz.label: WHAT THE CHECKLIST COVERS
production_viz.caption: checks the list, not whether it's good enough

beats.narration_text: Claude isn't judging whether the agreement is good enough — it's checking the SKILL.md's list of required clauses, one step at a time, and only doing what that file says.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm about to sign a vendor's Data Processing Agreement. Give me the fixed list of clauses I should check for before I sign — for each clause, tell me what it's supposed to do, what wording actually satisfies it, and the specific failure mode when it's missing or weak. Flag the two clauses that go missing most often in vendor DPAs. Go deeper: take the highest-stakes clause and rewrite a weak, real-world example of it into wording that would actually protect me.
